name: Casiodoro de Reina
title: Casiodoro de Reina: the Bear Bible and the service of translation
description: The 1569 Bear Bible and Casiodoro de Reina: a story of Spanish translation documented by the National Library of Spain (BNE) and the Complutense University of Madrid.

sections.heading: A Spanish Bible printed in Basel
paragraphs: In 1569, Casiodoro de Reina’s Bible translation, known as the Biblia del Oso (the Bear Bible), appeared in Basel. The National Library of Spain preserves and describes this edition among its collections of early printed books. The image of a bear on the title page gave the work the name by which many readers know it.

The BNE’s catalog record explains that the edition does not state all its printing details in the usual way and places its production in the context of Protestant printing in Basel. The copy is a material witness: its title page, its date and its makeup allow us to study the history of the translation without relying on a legend about the translator.

sections.heading: Reading an inheritance carefully
paragraphs: The Historical Library of the Complutense University presents Reina as a Hieronymite monk persecuted by the Inquisition for his ties to the Reformation. His project belonged to the sixteenth-century experience of exile and religious conflict. In that setting, putting the Scriptures into Spanish carried a personal cost and a lasting importance.

The library collections make it possible to distinguish the 1569 edition from later revisions. The name Reina-Valera reflects a history of translation and revision, not a single unchanged publication. Nor should we forget that there were earlier Spanish translations: the catalogs clarify what is meant by a complete version and by a printed edition.

reflection: Nehemiah 8:1–8 describes the reading of the law before the people and the effort to help them understand it. That passage invites us to think of translation as a task aimed at the reader’s understanding. A book can be physically within reach and still be hard to understand if no one works carefully on its language, its presentation and its explanation.

Gratitude for the Bear Bible can go together with the study of the original texts and of other translations. Respecting an inheritance does not require us to attribute perfection to every decision of those who passed it on. For the Spanish-speaking church, this story is a reminder of the value of teaching clearly and of keeping the memory of those who made that access possible.
review_note: The facsimile is not copied, and no later edition is proclaimed perfect. The absolute claim of a “first Spanish Bible,” without qualifying earlier works, is avoided.
